title: Links and Images
summary: Connect pages using anchor links and embed accessible images with proper attributes and path handling.
body: # Links and Images The real power of the World Wide Web comes from hyperlinks that connect documents across the globe, combined with rich visual media. In HTML, the anchor element (``) creates links, while the image element (``) displays graphical assets. ## Creating Hyperlinks with the Anchor Tag The anchor tag uses the `href` attribute (Hypertext Reference) to specify where the link points. You can navigate between internal pages of your own site or connect to external resources on other domains. ```html Visit MDN Web Docs About Our Project ``` When linking externally with `target="_blank"`, always add `rel="noopener noreferrer"` to protect security and performance. ## Embedding Accessible Images The `` tag is a void (self-closing) element. It requires two fundamental attributes: 1. `src`: The source location of the image file (URL or relative path). 2. `alt`: The alternative text description that displays if the image fails to load and is announced to visually impaired users by screen readers. ```html ``` Writing descriptive alt text is a strict accessibility requirement. Never leave alt text empty unless the image is purely decorative, in which case an empty string (`alt=""`) tells assistive devices to skip it. ## Relative vs Absolute Paths - Absolute paths provide the full protocol and domain (e.g., `https://example.com/logo.png`). - Relative paths point to files in relation to the current document (e.g., `./assets/photo.jpg` or `../styles.css`). ## Key takeaways - Anchor (``) tags connect pages using the required `href` attribute. - Use `rel="noopener noreferrer"` whenever opening external links in a new tab. - Every `` element must include a descriptive `alt` attribute for accessibility. - Choose relative paths for internal assets and absolute URLs for external resources.
